title: The Monadia Cycle
note: One fixed novel, retold every season with that season's Chogs and events: an original homage to the shape of classic portal fantasy (a lantern door, a long winter, a prophecy, a guardian beast's sacrifice and return, four thrones). No text, names or characters are taken from any other work. {pointer} is filled from the simulation; [[pointer|text]] appears only when the pointer has a value. Titles carry no numbers: chapters are numbered in the order they were written. See src/sim3/novel.ts.

chapters.title: The Lantern at the Crossroads
chapters.text:
This is a story about something that happened to one thousand nine hundred and sixty-nine Chogs on the same night, and if you have never heard of Chogs you will have to take my word for it that they are small, and purple, and braver than they look.

None of them meant to go anywhere. {w1} was in {w1home}, or rather was in a warm bed dreaming of {w1home}, when a light came on at the back of the dream. It was not a bright light. It was the sort of light you see under a door when somebody in the next room is still awake and you would very much like to know why. {w1} got up, the way you do in dreams, and opened the door.

On the other side there was snow.

It was falling quietly over a crossroads where four roads met, and in the very middle of the crossroads stood a lantern on a tall iron post, burning all by itself with nobody to tend it. The snow did not settle on the glass. It never would. {w1} stood under the lantern with bare feet and a slip of paper in one paw that had not been there a moment before, and on the paper was a single word: {w1job}.

A little way off, {w2} was standing under the same lantern, or under another lantern exactly like it (nobody has ever settled that question), holding a slip that said {w2job}. And somewhere beyond the falling snow {w3} of {w3home} was reading the word {w3job} for the second time, very slowly, the way you read a letter from someone you have not met yet.

That was how it began. Not with trumpets. With a lantern, and snow, and a great many small creatures reading their own names for a new life by a light that nobody had lit.

This is Season {season} of the Monadia Cycle.

chapters.title: The Grey Hush
chapters.text:
The snow, they soon learned, was not ordinary snow.

It had been falling on Monadia for a whole season before they came, and it would keep falling until something was done about it. The bells in the towers had frozen in their frames and would not ring. The rivers ran slow and silver under a skin of ice. The fruit in the market orchards hung hard and glassy on the branches, as if the trees were holding their breath. The old folk of the towns, the ones who had been there before the summoning and had forgotten how they got there, called it the Grey Hush, and they said it in whispers, the way you mention a cold that might be listening.

Far to the south, past the Field of Broken Wallets, a castle of black glass stood on a dark hill with one window lit. In that window sat {king}, and {king} was the reason for the Hush. Nobody had ever seen the Demon King smile, but everybody agreed that the cold got worse when the Demon King was pleased.

Around the castle, the old folk said, the Demon King had set four seals, and on each seal sat a general. {g1} held the seal of {r1}, where the volcanoes smoked under the snow. {g2} held the seal of {r2}, under the black water of the coast. {g3} held the seal of {r3}, among a thousand mirrors that showed everything except the truth. And {g4} held the seal of {r4}, where the meadows slept and dreamed the same bad dream every night.

"While the four seals hold," said the old folk, "the Hush holds. And while the Hush holds, nothing new can grow."

Then they would look at the newcomers, standing in the snow with their slips of paper, and something in their faces would change. It was not quite hope. It was the look of someone who has been waiting a very long time for a knock on the door, and has just heard one.

chapters.title: The Guild Opens
chapters.text:
There is a kind of courage that does not look like courage at all. It looks like getting up in the morning and going to work.

The guild halls of Monadia opened their doors on the first grey dawn, and the boards inside filled with notices: slimes in the river reeds, wolves at the high pass, a baker's cart that needed guarding through the woods, a town gate split by the frost that needed mending before nightfall. None of it was the kind of thing that ends up in songs. All of it needed doing.

The first to come back with a stamped quest was {firstQuester}, the {firstQuesterJob}, carrying proof of "{firstQuest}" all the way from {firstQuestPlace}. {firstQuester} was cold to the bone and had lost one boot to a snowdrift and did not care in the slightest. The guild clerk, an elderly Chog who had stamped nothing for a whole season, brought the stamp down so hard that the inkwell jumped, and the sound rang through the hall like the first note of a bell that has been frozen too long.

By the end of that first day {questsDone} quests had been turned in. Strangers who had woken under the lantern that morning were sharing soup and maps and opinions about the proper way to fight a slime. [[cand1|Already one name kept coming up more than the others, and that name was {cand1}.]]

And here is the curious thing, which nobody noticed at the time. Wherever a quest had been finished, the snow fell a little more softly.

chapters.title: Two for the Road
chapters.text:
It is one thing to be brave on your own. It is another thing, and a better one, to be brave with somebody.

{partyA} had been staring at the notice for "{partyQuest}" for a long time, reading it and putting it back and reading it again, when {partyB} came and stood alongside and read it too.

"It says two would be better than one," said {partyB}.

"It doesn't say that," said {partyA}.

"It would, if it were honest," said {partyB}, and took the notice off the board.

They set out together into the grey morning, and they argued for the first mile about which road to take, and for the second mile about whose fault it was that they had taken the wrong one, and by the third mile they had stopped arguing and started talking, which is how most friendships that are worth anything begin.

The old folk watched them go from the doorway of the guild hall. "That's how the Hush ends," said one of them, though she could not have told you why she thought so. "Not all at once. Two by two."

chapters.title: Smoke on the Horizon
chapters.text:
The first raid came at dusk, the way the old songs said it would, though nobody had believed the old songs until then.

{raidSize} demons poured out of the grey toward {raidTown}: imps with pitchforks and too many teeth, dark knights with patient spears, a cultist or two chanting in a language that made the snow fall upward for a moment and then think better of it. The town bell, frozen in its tower all season, could not ring. So the townsfolk banged on pots instead, which is less dignified but works just as well.

{raidOutcome}

In the morning there was a new notice nailed to every guild board in Monadia, written in letters so large that even the imps could have read it, if any had been foolish enough to come close: DEFEND YOUR TOWNS. Nobody needed to be told that the story had changed. You could feel it in the cold. The Demon King had noticed them.

chapters.title: The Temple of Small Lights
chapters.text:
Not every quest ends well. That is something the old songs leave out, and they are wrong to.

{firstFallen} was carried back from "{firstFallenQuest}" on a stretcher made of two spears and somebody's coat, and laid down in the nearest temple among the candles. Temples in Monadia are small and warm and smell of wax and old wood, and the healers who work there do not ask how you got hurt. They only ask where.

It was a long night. Outside, the Hush pressed against the windows like a grey animal trying to get in. Inside, a healer sat beside {firstFallen} and lit one candle after another, and every time a candle was lit the frost on the nearest window drew back a little, as if it did not like to be looked at.

"Will I be all right?" asked {firstFallen}, in the small hours.

"You will be all right," said the healer, "and then you will go out and do something foolish again, and then you will come back here, and I will light more candles. That's how it works. That's how it has always worked."

And by morning {firstFallen} was sitting up and asking for breakfast, which, as every healer knows, is the surest sign of all.

chapters.title: The Generals Wake
chapters.text:
On the second grey dawn the ground shook in four places at once, and every Chog in Monadia felt it in their teeth.

In {r1}, {g1} stepped out of the dungeon mouth and looked up at the falling snow as if it owed them money. In {r2}, {g2} rose out of the black water without making a ripple and stood dripping on the shore, listening. In {r3}, {g3} walked out of a thousand mirrors at once and smiled a thousand smiles, none of them kind. And in {r4}, {g4} began to sing a lullaby that nobody could ever remember afterwards, though everyone who heard it slept badly for a week.

The Demon Generals were awake, and each of them sat upon a seal, and the seals hummed under them like hives.

The guild boards changed again that morning. New notices appeared at the very top, written in red ink that would not freeze: FACE THE GENERAL OF LIQUIDATION. SILENCE THE DROWNED ARCHIVIST. SHATTER THE MIRROR WRAITH. WAKE FROM THE NIGHTMARE SHEPHERD.

Most Chogs read them, swallowed hard, and went back to the slime quests. That is nothing to be ashamed of. But a few did not go back. A few stood in front of those red notices for a long time, very still, the way you stand at the edge of cold water before you decide to jump.

chapters.title: Supper at the Baker's House
chapters.text:
If you are ever lost in a strange country in the middle of a long winter, the best thing that can happen to you is to be asked in for supper.

It happened to {w1} and {w2} on the evening of the second day, when the snow was coming down thick and blue in the dusk and they had quite given up on finding the inn. A round door opened in a round house at the edge of town, and a round baker with flour up to the elbows looked out at them and said, "Well, you'd better come in, hadn't you, before you turn into snowmen," and that was that.

There was bread, of course, hot from the oven, with the steam still coming out of it when you broke it open. There was soup with things in it that you could not name and did not need to. There was a pot of something sweet and dark for afterwards, and a fire that cracked and popped like it was telling jokes. [[w3|Halfway through the soup the door opened again and {w3} came in, stamping snow off their feet, saying they had followed the smell of bread across half the town.]]

And when the plates were empty and the fire had settled down, the baker told them the rhyme. Every child in Monadia knows it, the baker said, though few of them know what it means:

When the four seals crack and the grey frost thaws,
When the Lynx walks under the lantern's light,
The smallest word shall break the black glass throne,
And four shall sit where one sat alone.

"What does it mean?" asked {w1}.

The baker looked at the slip of paper sticking out of {w1}'s pocket, the one with the word {w1job} on it, and smiled in a way that made the fire seem warmer. "I think," said the baker, "that it means you."

chapters.title: The Lynx Walks Again
chapters.text:
{levelFive} was the first in all Monadia to reach the fifth level of their calling, and on the night it happened, something walked out of the snow.

It was a lynx. That is the simplest way to say it, and the least true. It was as big as a pony and as silver as starlight on water, and where its paws touched the snow the snow turned for a moment into the green of new grass and then, reluctantly, back into snow again. Its eyes were the colour of the sky just before morning. It did not look at {levelFive} the way an animal looks at you. It looked the way a very old friend looks at you, when you have done something they always knew you could do.

"Who are you?" whispered {levelFive}, who was the {levelFiveJob} and had never in their life expected to be spoken to by anything so large.

"I am Orrun," said the lynx, and its voice was so deep that the snow on the rooftops slid off all at once. "I was here before the Hush, and I will be here after it. I walk where the brave are walking. Tonight, I walk with you."

And then it was gone, and there were only paw prints in the snow, and in each paw print, for a little while, a single blade of green grass.

By morning the news was in every town. Nobody quite knew who had started it. But they were saying it in the markets and in the guild halls and in the temples among the candles, and even the old folk, who had stopped believing in most things, said it under their breath: the Lynx walks again.

chapters.title: A Name Spoken in the Dark
chapters.text:
Some enemies you choose. Some choose you.

{nemesisA} had gone into the dungeon twice to face {nemesisBoss}, and twice had been carried out again, cold and quiet, to wake among the candles of the nearest temple. The second time, {nemesisA} did not ask for breakfast. {nemesisA} lay very still and looked at the ceiling, and the healers, who had seen that look before, left a candle burning by the bed and did not say anything at all.

In the night {nemesisA} said a name out loud, once, to the dark. It was the name of the general. It was not said in fear. It was said the way you write something down so that you will not forget it.

Outside, the snow kept falling. But if you had been standing in the temple yard just then, and if you had been very patient, you might have seen something silver pause at the edge of the lantern light, and listen, and go on its way.

chapters.title: The Long Road
chapters.text:
There is a part of every journey that the songs skip, because it is long and cold and nothing much happens in it. That part is where most of the courage is.

For days the people of Monadia worked under the grey sky. They carried letters between frozen towns. They forged blades in smithies where the fire was the only warm thing for a mile. They baked, and fished through holes in the ice, and dug in the iron-hard fields, and walked the long roads between the dungeons with their maps folded small inside their coats. One hundred quests turned into two hundred, and two hundred into more, and by the time anybody thought to count, {questsDone} quests had been turned in at the guild halls of Monadia.

The bards had started to keep lists. At the top of most lists were {cand1}, {cand2} and {cand3}. [[rivalA|And in the training yards, where the snow had been trampled into slush, everybody was talking about {rivalA} and {rivalB}, who had fought each other {rivalCount} times and still refused to call it a rivalry.]]

And the snow, if you watched it closely, which almost nobody did, was falling a little more slowly than before.

chapters.title: Interlude: A Quarter of the Way
chapters.text:
A quarter of the season is gone. Here is how Monadia stands, written down plainly, the way the guild clerks write it in their ledgers.

Quests completed: {questsDone}. Raids held: {raidsHeld}. Raids lost: {raidsLost}. [[mostRaided|The town that has suffered most is {mostRaided}, raided {mostRaidedCount} times.]]

The names on everyone's lips are {cand1} ({cand1job}), {cand2} ({cand2job}) and {cand3} ({cand3job}).

The four seals hold. The Hush holds. But in the orchards outside the capital, one gardener swears that a single apple has turned from glass back into fruit, and is willing to show it to anybody who asks, and a great many people have asked.

chapters.title: The Candied Promise
chapters.text:
Now I must tell you about {traitor}, and I would rather not, but a story that leaves out the hard parts is not a story worth telling.

{traitor} was {traitorJobA}, and a good one, and nobody would have guessed. But {traitor} was tired of the cold, and tired of the long roads, and most of all tired of hearing other names in the songs. And one evening, at the edge of a frozen wood, a cultist in a dark hood stepped out from between the trees with a little silver box in one hand.

Inside the box were candied moonberries, glittering like frost, and the smell of them was the smell of summer.

"The Demon King knows your name," said the cultist softly. "The Demon King thinks you are wasted on bakers' carts and slime quests. Come to the castle. There is a warm room there, and as many of these as you like, and a place at the King's right hand when the others have given up. Only tell us which roads the parties take to the dungeons. That's all. Such a little thing."

{traitor} ate one moonberry, and then another, and then, without really meaning to, told them everything.

It is a strange thing about candied moonberries. The more of them you eat, the hungrier you get. By the time {traitor} reached the black glass castle, the warm room turned out to be a cell, and the cultist had stopped smiling, and somewhere far behind, on the roads {traitor} had betrayed, the parties were walking into ambushes.

The Demon King did not even come down to look. The Demon King only said, from the lit window, "Keep that one. It may be useful."

chapters.title: The First Seal
chapters.text:
{slain} had held {slainRegion} for days. Parties went in. Parties were carried out. The temple candles in that country burned day and night.

Then {slayer} went in.

{slayer} was {slayerJobA}, level {slayerLevel}, and nobody had bet on them. The fight in the dungeon lasted longer than anyone waiting outside could bear. Some of them swore afterwards that they heard a sound from deep underground like a bell that had been frozen for a hundred years, cracking.

When it was over, the dungeon was quiet, and the first seal lay broken on the stone floor like a dropped plate.

[[slayerNemesis|{slayer} had faced {slain} before, twice, and twice been carried out. This time {slayer} walked out on their own feet.]]

And outside, all across {slainRegion}, for the first time in a whole season, it began to drip. It was only a little drip, from the very end of one icicle on the dungeon gate. But the whole crowd stood and watched it, in perfect silence, as if it were the most beautiful thing they had ever seen. Which, in a way, it was.

Far to the south, in the black glass castle, {king} felt something give, and for the first time that season, frowned.

chapters.title: The Peddler of Stars
chapters.text:
The night after the first seal broke, a sleigh came down out of the sky.

It was pulled by nothing that anybody could see, and it jingled with bells that were not frozen, and it was driven by a tall figure in a coat the colour of the space between stars. The figure stopped in the middle of every town square in Monadia, which should have been impossible, and was not, and opened a pack that seemed to have no bottom.

"I am the Peddler of Stars," said the figure. "I do not come while the Hush is whole. But it has cracked tonight, and the Constellations who watch over this land have sent me with gifts."

The gifts were not for everybody. They were for the Chogs whom the Constellations had chosen, the ones who were watched over by the bright patient eyes in the sky. To one the Peddler gave a skill, wrapped in starlight, that would make a blade faster or a prayer stronger or a forge hotter. To another the Peddler gave a quest, folded small, with a road on it that nobody else could see. [[cand1|{cand1}, it is said, received something too, but never told anyone what it was.]]

"These are tools, not toys," said the Peddler, closing the pack. "Use them well. The winter is cracked, not broken."

And then the sleigh was gone, and the bells with it, and every Chog who had been given something stood in the snow holding it carefully, the way you hold something you did not know you were waiting for.

chapters.title: Not a Knight
chapters.text:
{underdog} was the {underdogJob}, and the {underdogJob} is not the sort of calling that ends up in songs.

But {underdog} kept turning up. At the guild hall at dawn. At the town wall when the demons came. At the temple, helping to carry the stretchers. On the long road between the dungeons, with a pack that was always heavier than it needed to be because {underdog} always carried something extra for somebody else.

And one morning the bards looked at their lists and found that {underdog} was on them, near the top, among the knights and mages and sword-saints, and nobody could quite remember when that had happened.

"Not a knight," said one bard, scratching their head.

"Not a mage either," said another.

"No," said the old baker, who happened to be passing with a tray of loaves. "Not a knight. Not a mage. The smallest word." And the baker went on down the street humming the old rhyme, and left the bards to argue about it.

chapters.title: The Walls of {siegeTown}
chapters.text:
The demons came back to {siegeTown} again, and again, and again.

Nobody knew why the Demon King hated that town in particular. Perhaps there was no reason. Perhaps it was only that {siegeTown} had held once, at the beginning, and the Demon King was not used to being refused. Whatever the cause, the raids kept coming, and the people of {siegeTown} grew tired, and then grew angry, and then, which is the most dangerous thing of all for a besieger, grew clever.

They built walls out of anything they could find: old carts, barrels of frozen fish, the bakery's spare ovens, a statue of a long-forgotten mayor. They taught their children to ring the pot-bells. They put candles in every window so that the town would never be dark. And when the next raid came, the demons found a town that was waiting for them.

The children of {siegeTown} still play a game called Raid, in which half of them are demons and half of them are defenders. The defenders always win. That is the rule.

chapters.title: The Second Seal
chapters.text:
News of the first seal travelled fast, and courage travels faster than news.

In {slainRegion} the parties grew bigger, and the songs grew louder, and the snow grew soft and wet and heavy, the kind of snow that makes good snowballs and bad roads. It was {slayer}, the {slayerJob}, who struck the blow that finally brought {slain} down, and the second seal broke with a noise like river ice in spring.

[[slayerRival|Somewhere in the crowd that cheered, {slayerRival} cheered loudest of all, and only a little bit jealously.]]

That night the rivers began to move again under their ice. You could hear them if you lay awake: a deep, slow grinding, like the world turning over in its sleep. The Demon King sent more raiders, and more, and it did not help, because the people of Monadia had stopped being afraid of the dark. They had seen what was on the other side of it.

chapters.title: Interlude: Halfway
chapters.text:
Halfway. The seals: {seals} of 4 broken.

Monadia has completed {questsDone} quests, held its walls {raidsHeld} times and lost them {raidsLost} times. [[siegeTown|{siegeTown} has been besieged so often that its children play "raid" the way other children play tag.]]

The hero candidates have changed. Now it is {cand1} ({cand1job}), {cand2} ({cand2job}) and {cand3} ({cand3job}). The bards have started writing whole songs, which is always a bad sign for somebody.

And in the black glass castle, in a cold cell at the bottom of a cold stair, {traitor} has stopped eating moonberries, and has started to cry.

chapters.title: The Altar of Four Winds
chapters.text:
On a hill between the four countries, where the winds from all four directions meet and argue, there stands a great flat stone with old writing on its sides. Nobody living can read the writing. It is called the Altar of Four Winds, and on the night I am going to tell you about, the Demon King came down from the black glass castle and stood beside it, with {traitor} in chains.

"The old law is written on this stone," said {king}, and the cold in that voice made the stars shiver. "Every betrayer belongs to me. Every one. You know the law, Lynx. You were there when it was carved."

Orrun had come out of the dark without anybody seeing, and stood at the foot of the hill, silver and silent.

"I know the law," said Orrun.

"Then you know I will keep this one," said {king}. "Unless."

Nobody heard what was said after that. The two of them spoke alone, by the altar, for a long time, while {traitor} shivered in the snow and the demons waited in a ring with their torches. And when they had finished, the Demon King laughed, which was a terrible sound, and struck off {traitor}'s chains, and {traitor} ran.

Orrun lay down upon the stone.

I will not tell you all of what happened next. It is enough to say that the demons were cruel, as demons are, and that Orrun did not fight them, though Orrun could have scattered them all like dry leaves, and that when the torches had gone back up the road to the castle the great silver lynx lay very still upon the altar, and did not move, and the snow fell on that silver fur and did not melt.

{traitor} had not run far. {traitor} had hidden behind a rock at the bottom of the hill and seen all of it, and stayed there all night in the snow, and did not stop crying until the stars went out.

chapters.title: Morning at the Broken Altar
chapters.text:
Just before dawn there was a sound like the whole sky clearing its throat.

{traitor} looked up from behind the rock. The Altar of Four Winds had cracked from end to end, a great split right down the middle of the old stone, and the old writing on its sides was glowing gold. And the altar was empty.

Then something warm breathed on the back of {traitor}'s neck.

Orrun was standing there, bigger than before, if that were possible, and brighter, and where Orrun stood the snow was gone and the grass was green and there were flowers in it, small blue ones, the kind that come at the very beginning of spring.

"But you were," said {traitor}, and could not finish.

"There is an older law than the one on that stone," said Orrun, "carved before the Demon King was anything at all. When someone who has done no wrong gives themselves freely in a betrayer's place, the stone itself breaks, and what was dead comes walking back." The lynx bent its great head. "Now. You have work to do. Go back to the others. Tell them everything. And then fight beside them."

"They'll never forgive me," said {traitor}.

"Some of them will," said Orrun. "That is generally how it goes. Run along."

And {traitor} ran, all the way back to the guild hall, through snow that was turning to rain, and told them everything, and some of them did forgive, and that was generally how it went.

chapters.title: The Third Seal
chapters.text:
{slain} was the cleverest of the four, and the cruellest. It did not matter.

{slayer} stood in the wreckage of the dungeon of {slainRegion}, breathing hard, while the third seal crumbled to dust between their paws. [[slayerSponsor|Above them, very high, a single star flared brighter than all the rest. In the towns they had started calling it the star of {slayerSponsor}, because that was the Constellation who had believed in {slayer} first.]]

When {slayer} came up out of the dungeon, it was raining. Not snowing. Raining. Warm, ordinary, beautiful rain that ran off the roofs and filled the gutters and washed the grey out of the air. All across Monadia the frozen bells began to drip and creak in their towers, and in one town, just one, a bell rang all by itself, very softly, once.

One seal remains. Everyone knows which one. Everyone knows it will be the hardest.

chapters.title: The Last Seal
chapters.text:
The last general, {slain}, did not wait in the dungeon. It came out to meet them.

What happened in {slainRegion} that day is told a hundred different ways in the taverns of Monadia, and in every version {slayer} is the one still standing at the end. Some say Orrun was there, silver at the edge of the battle, though nobody saw the lynx strike a single blow. Some say {traitor} was there, fighting harder than anybody, as if trying to pay back something that could never quite be paid. Most say both.

The fourth seal broke with a sound like a bell cracking in the coldest part of winter, and then every bell in Monadia, every single one, in every tower in every town, began to ring at once.

The Grey Hush was over.

I wish you could have seen it. The snow did not melt so much as surrender. It slid off the roofs and ran down the streets and poured into the rivers, which roared and burst their ice and ran laughing down to the sea. Glass fruit turned into real fruit on the branches. Green came up through the slush in every field. People who had not seen the sun in a whole season stood in the streets with their faces turned up, eyes closed, and did not say anything at all.

Between the people of Monadia and the Demon King, there was now nothing but a long road south, and whatever courage they had left.

chapters.title: The March
chapters.text:
They did not all go. Bakers stayed to bake; somebody had to. Farmers stayed with their fields, which were waking up and needed watching. The healers stayed in the temples and lit candles for the ones who went.

But from every town, in twos and threes and whole loud parties, Chogs walked south. {cand1} went. {cand2} went. {cand3} went, saying it was only to watch, and fooling nobody. [[traitor|{traitor} went too, at the very back, where nobody would have to look at them, until somebody dropped back and walked alongside, and then somebody else, and by the end of the first day {traitor} was not at the back any more.]]

Orrun walked at the front. Nobody had asked the lynx to. Nobody needed to.

The black glass castle stood on its dark hill exactly as the old stories said, one window lit. But the hill was not dark any more. Green was creeping up it from the bottom, a little higher every hour, like a tide. And when the first party reached the gate, {king} stood up from the throne for the first time in the whole season.

"Again," said the Demon King, very quietly. "Always again."

chapters.title: Interlude: Three Quarters
chapters.text:
Three quarters of the season are gone. The Demon King still stands at {kingHp}% strength.

The march goes on. Parties go up the black hill and come back down on stretchers, and go up again. The temple candles burn all night. [[rivalA|{rivalA} and {rivalB} are said to have stopped arguing, which worries everyone.]]

The candidates now: {cand1}, {cand2} and {cand3}. One of them, or someone nobody has noticed yet, is about to become a legend.

And the old baker, who has walked all the way south with a basket of bread for the troops, is telling anyone who will listen: "The smallest word. You'll see. The smallest word."

chapters.title: Last Stand
chapters.text:
Time ran short. The season was ending and the Demon King was still on the throne.

That night every star over Monadia burned at once. The Constellations, all of them, the patient bright eyes that had watched over this country since before the Hush, poured their light down into the people below. Swords cut deeper. Shields held longer. Every blow against {king} struck three times as hard.

Orrun stood on the hill below the castle and lifted that great silver head, and roared, and the roar went out across Monadia from one end to the other, and every Chog who heard it, wherever they were, felt their heart beat once, very hard, like a door being knocked on.

It was not fair. It was not meant to be. It was the Last Stand.

chapters.title: The Final Blow
chapters.text:
In the end it was not a knight, or not necessarily. It was {hero}.

{hero} had woken under the lantern at the crossroads as {heroJobA} of {heroHome}, at level 1, with bare feet and a slip of paper with one small word on it. At level {heroLevel}, standing in the throne room of the black glass castle with the walls cracking all around and the green coming in through the cracks, {hero} landed the blow that put {king}, the Demon King, on the floor.

[[heroCompanion|{heroCompanion} was beside them. {heroCompanion} had been beside them for most of the season, on the long roads and the cold nights, and was not going to be anywhere else for this.]] [[heroRival|{heroRival}, their rival, was the first to lift them onto their shoulders.]] [[heroSponsor|And high above, the star of {heroSponsor}, the Constellation who had believed in them first, burned brighter than all the rest.]]

The throne of black glass cracked from top to bottom. The one lit window went dark, and then, slowly, filled with ordinary morning.

Orrun came up the stair last of all, and the great silver lynx looked at {hero} for a long moment, the way a very old friend looks at you.

"The smallest word," said Orrun. "I always knew."

{hero}, {heroJob}, is the Hero of Season {season}.

chapters.title: The Spire of Four Thrones
chapters.text:
There is a spire in the middle of the Hive Capital, the tallest thing in all Monadia, and at the top of it there is a round room with four thrones in it. The thrones had been empty for longer than anybody could remember. The old folk said they were waiting.

They stopped waiting on the third day after the Demon King fell.

The whole of Monadia came to the coronation: smiths and bakers and farmers and fishers, soldiers in their best armour, mages in their best hats, healers who had not slept in a week and did not care. Orrun walked up the long stair first, and the four followed: {hero}, the Hero, and beside them {cand1}, {cand2} and {cand3}, who had been the names on everyone's lips all season long.

The old baker, who had insisted on being allowed to carry the crowns, set them on four heads one after another, and said the words that are said at such times, which I will not write down here because they are not mine to write.

And then there was a feast that went on for three days, and music that went on for four, and in the middle of it all {traitor} stood up, with everybody watching, and raised a cup to {hero}, and {hero} raised one back, and nobody said anything about candied moonberries ever again.

That is what the rhyme meant, you see. Four shall sit where one sat alone.

chapters.title: Epilogue: The White Stag
chapters.text:
They reigned well, the four of them, for what felt like a very long time and may have been only a day. That is how time works in Monadia, and it is best not to think about it too hard.

They carved the names into the Hall of Heroes: {hero}, Season {season}. Beside it, smaller, the ones who broke the seals: {slayers}. Below those, the ones the bards would not stop singing about. In all, Monadia completed {questsDone} quests that season, held its walls {raidsHeld} times and lost them {raidsLost} times, and every one of those numbers is somebody's story.

Then one evening, so the story goes, word came that a white stag had been seen in the woods at the edge of the capital, a stag that grants a wish to whoever catches it. And the four rode out after it, laughing, through the green woods and the long gold light, deeper and deeper, until the trees grew strange and close and the light went blue, and there in front of them, in a little clearing, stood a lantern on a tall iron post, burning all by itself with nobody to tend it.

They looked at one another. And then, one by one, they walked toward the light.

Somewhere, in a warm bed, a Chog woke up from a dream with a slip of paper in one paw. And on the slip of paper was a word. And it was a different word this time.

Far to the south, a window lit.

The Monadia Cycle turns.
